candidates.title: Outputs that the rollup interface allows (up to the 2 MiB tx buffer) cannot be executed on-chain: Application.executeOutput needs the full output bytes in calldata, and above about 419 KB (nonzero bytes) the transaction needs more than the EIP-7825 per-transaction gas cap because of the EIP-7623 calldata floor. Above about 126 KB it already exceeds the 128 KiB public-mempool transaction size. Nothing bounds output size to what a transaction can carry, unlike A3's bound for inputs

candidates.description: A5 requires: 'Conversely, the referee accepts every output that the settled state commits to, whenever its valid proof is presented. No party can make it stop accepting them.' For a voucher or delegate-call voucher, the only acceptance path that has an effect is Application.executeOutput(bytes output, OutputValidityProof proof), which takes the exact encoded output bytes as calldata. validateOutputHash accepts a hash of any size, but it executes nothing. The guest side (libcmt cmt_rollup_emit_voucher / emit_delegate_call_voucher / emit_notice, and the manual's rollup interface) lets an output use the whole 2 MiB CMIO tx buffer. On Ethereum after Fusaka/Prague, a transaction carrying N calldata bytes costs at least 21000 + 10*(zero bytes + 4*nonzero bytes) gas (EIP-7623 floor), and no transaction may use more than 2^24 = 16,777,216 gas (EIP-7825). So any voucher whose encoding has more than about 418,900 nonzero bytes (about 1.67 MB if all zero, less after executeOutput's quadratic memory cost of copying the payload into the outgoing call) can never be executed. Its valid proof cannot be presented in any transaction. Above about 126 KB (128 KiB minus the 63-sibling proof and ABI overhead) the transaction also exceeds the txpool size limit of geth and reth, so the public mempool does not relay it. For inputs, A3 bounds the input record so that the honest delivery proof fits ('It accepts no input so large that the honest proof of its delivery would exceed the chain's per-transaction limits'), and the InputBox enforces 64 KiB. Outputs have no counterpart: the rollups contracts, libcmt and the manual do not bound outputs to what an executeOutput transaction can carry, and nothing documents the limit. A settled, accepted output that the state commits to can therefore become permanently unexecutable.
candidates.trigger: The application guest emits a voucher or delegate-call voucher larger than about 419 KB nonzero (or about 126 KB for public-mempool relay), for example a batch-withdrawal multicall payload or data that it assembles from several inputs. The guest follows the documented rollup interface exactly: libcmt returns success and the output enters the outputs Merkle tree. An input sender can trigger it whenever the application builds an output whose size the sender influences across inputs (each input is at most 64 KiB, but outputs can aggregate them). After the epoch settles, anyone who calls executeOutput with the valid proof is refused by the chain's per-transaction limits.
candidates.reachability: Reachable from a valid template: the application guest writes any bytes into the tx buffer (any assignment of guest memory is presumed reachable), and libcmt accepts outputs up to the tx buffer size. The settled state's outputs Merkle root commits to the output, and DaveConsensus records that root at acceptance. The per-transaction limits come from the chain (EIP-7623 and EIP-7825 are active on Ethereum mainnet, which Dave names as its supported environment), not from any adversary.
candidates.rating_steps: 1. Out of scope? Partly arguable. The exclusion 'An application that is not correctly designed ... That exclusion covers only what such an application gets, which is its outputs' does not apply: the definition of a correctly designed application (section 2) constrains only the rollup interface and mcycle usage, not output size, and the manual documents outputs up to the tx buffer. 'Keeping outputs to prove them later is not on the honest operator's path' excludes the operator's storage, not the referee's acceptance. Nothing in the list excludes a referee that cannot accept a committed output. Not out of scope under the preferred reading. 2. Role: Application/LibOutputValidityProof are the 'cartesi-rollups-contracts 3.0.0-alpha.10 it pins (input box, output validation)', so Referee model, as the deployed referee. Section 3: 'A defect in what it accepts or derives is rated as if a deployed referee had it.' 3. High/Medium cases: none fits. It is not an unreachable-state case, not trailing data, not a support-only defect. 4. Critical: A5 is violated at a reachable state: 'Conversely, the referee accepts every output that the settled state commits to, whenever its valid proof is presented. No party can make it stop accepting them.' A valid proof exists but can never be presented. The section 8 Critical list also covers it: 'An honest proof or transaction that cannot fit the chain's per-transaction limits, other than the delivery proof of an input that A3 requires the input record to refuse' (the output proof is not an input delivery proof). R12 says 'Every transaction ... proofs included, fits the chain's per-transaction limits in the worst case of what it carries.' Claimed: Critical. 5. Alternative reading: if output execution is not an honest-operator transaction (R12 speaks of 'Every transaction the honest operator sends') and acceptance means only validateOutputHash, which works for any size, then executing oversized vouchers is the application's design choice. That gives Low, or Medium as an undocumented security-relevant limit, since the manual says 'Given the contents of an output, and a proof ... it is therefore possible to verify that the machine has in fact produced that output. This is how Cartesi Rollups settles disputes over the vouchers ...' and states no bound ('A contradiction between the manual and the behavior on a security-relevant point ... takes the severity it would have if the manual were right'). The deciding facts: whether A5's 'accepts' covers executing a voucher, and whether the Critical entry on honest proofs that cannot fit covers output proofs that any party presents.
candidates.claimed_severity: Critical (preferred: A5 and the section 8 entry on honest proofs that cannot fit) / Medium (undocumented limit contradicting the manual's 'it is possible to verify') / Low (if voucher size is the application's choice and only validateOutputHash counts as acceptance)
candidates.threat_to_goal: The goal says no adversary can make the application 'accept an output that the settled state does not commit to', and A5 adds the converse: every committed output stays acceptable. Here a correctly designed application (per section 2) settles the right state, but a voucher it emitted and the settled state commits to (such as a withdrawal) can never be executed. The funds it grants are stuck for good, and no party, honest or not, can present the proof. This is the output-side counterpart of the A3 input bound, which the deployment lacks.
candidates.evidence: Code reading: Application.executeOutput takes bytes calldata output and hashes it (validateOutput -> keccak256(output)). There is no size bound in Application, LibOutputValidityProof or libcmt (cmt_rollup_emit_voucher fails only with -ENOBUFS beyond the tx buffer). Chain experiment on a scratch anvil 1.5.1 (--hardfork osaka, port 8599, stopped afterwards): plain transactions to an EOA with N nonzero calldata bytes and gas limit 2^24. N=96,000 mined with gasUsed 3,861,000 = 21000+40N (the EIP-7623 floor applies). N=131,072: 5,263,880. N=300,000: 12,021,000. N=418,000: 16,741,000 (just under 2^24). N=420,000: stays pending, because floor 16,821,000 > 2^24. N=2,097,152: the node refuses the request ('Invalid request', body too large). An executeOutput call carries the output plus about 2.2 KB (63 siblings, index, offsets), plus execution gas (keccak, 63 hashes, memory expansion and the copy into the destination call), so the executable threshold is a little below 418,900 nonzero bytes. Anvil itself did not refuse gas limits above 2^24 in its pool; EIP-7825 is enforced by mainnet consensus and txpools.
candidates.test_idea: bugs/<ID>/test.sh: deploy the pinned rollups-contracts Application with a mock IOutputsMerkleRootValidator that accepts one root, on anvil with --hardfork osaka (or check the gas analytically against 2^24). Build in Lua (cartesi.hash-tree frontier, height 63) the outputs tree of one Voucher(destination, 0, payload) whose ABI encoding is 500,000 bytes of 0xab payload, and get its proof. Have the mock accept that root. Assert that eth_estimateGas of executeOutput(output, proof) is at most 2^24 and that the calldata is at most 131,072 bytes (the requirement under A5 and R12). Both fail today, so exit 1. A fixed deployment would bound output sizes (in libcmt/the manual and the referee, as A3 does for inputs) or provide an execution path that does not carry the bytes in one transaction; then the test emits the largest voucher the guest interface allows and the assertion holds. Equivalently, at the emulator/guest level: emit a voucher of maximal libcmt size from the baremetal emit-output guest and assert that 21000 + 40*len(executeOutput calldata) <= 2^24.

not_covered: No full on-chain Tournament.winLeafMatch transaction under the released constants with a 64 KiB InputBox input. Its gas was taken from earlier measurements (about 4.76 M step part, Dave's calibrated Gas.WIN_LEAF_MATCH 5.536 M) plus arithmetic: about 94,180 calldata bytes, an EIP-7623 floor of about 3.79 M, and 2x estimate about 11-13 M, under 2^24. The EIP-7623 floor was confirmed on anvil only for plain calldata transactions.

No new search for the worst-case uarch instruction count per mcycle (the 2^20-1 cap). By reading, the heaviest known cases (TLB flushes of 768 slots, soft-float/128-bit division emulated on the RV64I-only uarch, page walks with PMA scans, two flushes in one mcycle through an interrupt plus xRET) stay around 1e4-1e5, far below 1,048,575. Not measured.
